articles.headline: Neural Networks Are Already Clean
articles.blurb: The cause of polysemanticity in early model organisms was thought to be superposition. This convinced much of the field that networks pack concepts arbitrarily, but what looked like arbitrary packing was mostly recursive generalization, which is less concerning. This means networks can be studied directly, instead of needing to be untangled first. The outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than we thought.

articles.headline: The Gradient Is a Covariance
articles.blurb: Reinforcement learning, on-policy distillation, and supervised fine-tuning on near-policy data change only a small fraction of parameters. Small and sparse are different claims. The expected gradient is a covariance, the Fisher is a variance, and the Fisher caps the gradient for any reward. At one position, the Fisher is the variance of logit sensitivities: whatever moves every candidate together counts for nothing. None of this needs on-policy sampling - it needs a score centered under the sampling distribution.

articles.headline: Mo' turns, mo' problems
articles.blurb: Doing reinforcement learning for agent use-cases is conceptually not at all that complicated. For each problem, you set up a VM with a harness and a fresh model context, send the prompt, let the model make tool calls, score the whole thing at the end, and update the weights. Agentic post-training means there's more than the model to consider. Even when the harness is consistent, you can still go off-policy with the trajectories themselves. Agents spawn subagents, make parallel tool calls, and compact large sessions, which adds complexity.

As AI dramatically increases the volume and speed of production, documenting not just what a brand looks like but why and how its decisions should be made becomes essential for maintaining coherence.

articles.headline: Fit height to background pattern size with calc-size()
articles.blurb: CSS background patterns can end awkwardly when a container's content produces a height that isn't an exact multiple of the background tile, while `background-repeat: round` fixes the edge by distorting the pattern itself. Combining `calc-size()` with `round()` instead lets the browser calculate the element's natural height and round it up to the nearest multiple of the tile height. The result behaves similarly to `min-height`, preserving both the content-driven size and the original pattern proportions, though browser support remains limited.
